## 8. Structure of the code

### 8.1 Local consistency: the parity checks

Realisable signatures are far from arbitrary. The following rules involve five leaves at a time and are the analogue of local parity checks.

**Theorem 8.1 (Cherry propagation).** For any leaf order $\pi$ and leaves $a,b,c,d,e$: if $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,c,d) = 0$ and $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,c,e) = 0$ then $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,d,e) = 0$. In words: $ab|cd$ and $ab|ce$ force $ab|de$.

*Proof sketch.* Type $0$ on $(a,b,c,d)$ says the positions of $a,b$ are both below or both above those of $c,d$; the same for $c,e$. Combining the two systems of inequalities places $a,b$ on one side of both $d$ and $e$, which is type $0$ on $(a,b,d,e)$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.2 (Forbidden configuration).** No leaf order displays $ab|cd$, $ab|ce$ and $ac|de$ simultaneously. Hence the corresponding ternary word is not a codeword.

**Theorem 8.3 (Mixed rules).** For distinct leaves: $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,c,d) = 0$ and $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,c,e) = 1$ force $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,c,d,e) = 2$; and $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,c,d) = 0$ with $\mathrm{q}_\pi(a,b,c,e) = 2$ force $\mathrm{q}_\pi(b,c,d,e) = 2$.

All three rules are proved by translating the type characterisations into linear inequalities among the four or five positions and eliminating. An exhaustive scan over the $120$ five-leaf orders and all premise pairs on overlapping quadruples produces $210$ valid two-premise implications of this kind, of which the above are representatives.

### 8.2 The five-leaf code, counted exactly

**Theorem 8.4.** Exactly $15$ of the $3^5 = 243$ ternary words of length five arise as the quartet signature of a five-leaf tree, and
$$8 \cdot 15 = 120 = 5! .$$

Thus the code rate on five leaves is $\log_3(15)/5 \approx 0.493$: less than half the ambient ternary dimension is used. Any packing bound computed in the *unconstrained* cube is therefore far off, and it matters that the first-moment argument of Section 5 is carried out inside the realisable code (it samples trees, not words).

### 8.3 Symmetries and the packing bound

**Proposition 8.5 (Three symmetries).** The quartet signature of a caterpillar is unchanged by: (i) reversal of the leaf order, $\pi \mapsto \mathrm{rev} \circ \pi$; (ii) exchange of the two lowest positions; (iii) exchange of the two highest positions.

*Proof sketch.* (i) Reversal $v \mapsto (n-1)-v$ flips every comparison simultaneously, so every clause of Definition 3.1 is preserved — and this holds for all quadruples, degenerate ones included. (ii) Exchanging the values $0$ and $1$ preserves the type of every quadruple of distinct leaves, because the two swapped positions are the two global minima and hence remain the "low pair" of any quadruple containing both; a case analysis over the relative positions of the remaining leaves discharges the rest. (iii) is (ii) conjugated by (i). $\square$

**Theorem 8.6 (Packing bound).** For $n \geq 4$, the number of distinct caterpillar quartet signatures on $n$ leaves satisfies
$$8 \cdot |\mathcal{C}_n| \leq n! .$$

*Proof sketch.* Let $r$ be reversal, $a$ the exchange of the two lowest positions, $b = r a r$. The eight products of $\{1,r\}\times\{1,a\}\times\{1,b\}$ are pairwise distinct for $n \geq 4$, as one sees by evaluating each of them at the first and last position; by Proposition 8.5 each fibre of the signature map is a union of left cosets of this group of order eight acting freely on $S_n$, hence has size at least $8$. Summing the fibre sizes gives the bound. $\square$

Exhaustive computation gives $|\mathcal{C}_n| = 3, 15, 90, 630$ for $n = 4,5,6,7$, i.e. exactly $n!/8$ in each case: the signature map is precisely eight-to-one. Equality for all $n$ amounts to the statement that a caterpillar is reconstructible from its quartets up to its own automorphisms — the converse direction, which we do not prove here.

---

## 9. Algorithms and numerical results

### 9.1 Computing a signature

Given a leaf order $\pi$ on $n$ leaves, the signature is computed by iterating over the $\binom{n}{4}$ four-subsets and evaluating $\mathrm{code}_3$, at cost $O(n^4)$ arithmetic comparisons. This is the basic primitive of all computations below.

### 9.2 Verifying avoidance

To certify that a family $T_1,\dots,T_k$ has no common quartet, compute the $k$ signatures and scan for a constant coordinate: $O(k n^4)$ time. Certificates of this kind underlie Theorems 7.4 and 7.6.

### 9.3 Group-reduced exhaustive search

The identity $\mathrm{q}_\pi(\sigma a,\sigma b,\sigma c,\sigma d) = \mathrm{q}_{\pi\sigma}(a,b,c,d)$ reduces the verification of "every pair of $n$-leaf caterpillars shares a quartet" from $(n!)^2$ pairs to $n!$ single orders compared against the identity. For $n=6$ this is $720$ instead of $518400$ and makes the exhaustive proof of Theorem 7.5 feasible.

### 9.4 Local search for avoiding families

To probe the true growth of $h(k)$ we minimise the objective
$$\mathrm{cost}(T_1,\dots,T_k) := \#\{\,Q : \text{all } T_i \text{ agree on } Q \,\},$$
by randomised hill-climbing over transpositions of individual leaf orders, restarting from random families. A family with $\mathrm{cost} = 0$ is an avoidance certificate; repeated failure is evidence (not proof) that none exists.

### 9.5 Numerical summary

All of the following were obtained by direct computation.

| statement | value |
|---|---|
| type counts on a fixed quartet, $n=6$ | $240 : 240 : 240 = 6!/3$ each |
| agreement probability, $k$ caterpillars | exactly $3^{-(k-1)}$ for $k=2,3,4$; $n=4,5,6$ |
| distinct signatures, $n=4,5,6,7$ | $3,\,15,\,90,\,630$ ($=n!/8$) |
| six-leaf orders sharing no quartet with the identity | $0$ (out of $720$) |
| common quartets of the nine-leaf triple | $0$ (out of $126$) |
| largest full-distance ternary family, length $1..4$ | $3,3,3,3$ |
| largest avoiding leaf number found, $k = 2,3,4$ | $5,\ 9,\ 15$–$16$ |

The last row, extended by longer searches to $k=5,6$, gives largest avoiding leaf numbers around $20$ and $30$: the ratio between consecutive entries is close to $1.7$, comfortably above the certified $3^{1/4} \approx 1.32$ and far below the doubly exponential upper bound.

---

## 10. Discussion

### 10.1 What the dictionary buys

The reformulation does three concrete things.

1. **It makes agreement computable.** Agreement of trees on a four-set is equality of a single letter. This turns a statement about restrictions of split systems into a statement about a finite ternary array, which is why exhaustive verification at $n=6$ and $n=9$ is possible at all.

2. **It makes the first moment exact.** Because the three types are *exactly* equinumerous (Theorem 4.4), the probability of $k$-fold agreement is exactly $3^{-(k-1)}$ with no correction term. Every inefficiency in Corollary 5.4 is therefore attributable to the union bound over $n^4$ quadruples.

3. **It identifies the right notion of avoidance.** Theorem 6.1 rules out the distance formulation decisively. The correct object is a family of codewords with no constant coordinate — a *covering code* condition read across the family rather than a packing condition read pairwise.

### 10.2 The rate

Write $h(k) = \Theta(c^k)$ as the conjectural shape of the answer. Corollary 5.4 gives $c \geq 3^{1/4}$; the data of Section 9 suggest $c \approx 1.7$; a trivial counting argument places $c \leq 2$ if the empirical pattern persists, and in any case Theorem 7.3 gives only the doubly exponential $3^{2^k}$. In the coding language, $c$ is a **packing rate in a constrained ternary code**: the supremum of rates at which one can place words of the tree code $\mathcal{C}_n$ so that no coordinate is constant. Both the constrained nature of $\mathcal{C}_n$ (Section 8) and the many-body nature of the condition (Section 6) are essential features of this quantity, and neither is captured by classical rate–distance theory.

### 10.3 Where the upper bound loses

The iterated Erdős–Szekeres argument extracts a *global* monotone pattern once per tree, and each extraction squares the required leaf number. But a common quartet is a local object: it needs four leaves to line up, not a monotone chain through the whole leaf set. The natural replacement is a Ramsey-type theorem for $4$-uniform hypergraphs with three colours, applied directly to the ternary colouring of $\binom{[n]}{4}$ induced by the family. Since agreement is now literally a colour coincidence, such a theorem would be applied to the signature array rather than to the trees, and would plausibly replace $3^{2^k}$ by $c^k$.

---

## 11. Future work

* **Determine the rate.** Prove $h(k) \leq C c^{k}$ for some absolute $c$, closing the gap between $3^{(k-2)/4}$ and $3^{2^k}$. The plausible attack is a Ramsey argument on $4$-uniform three-coloured hypergraphs, exploiting the local consistency rules of Section 8 to restrict the colourings that can occur.
* **Sharpen the lower bound.** The union bound wastes a factor; a Lovász-local-lemma or entropy-compression treatment of the (highly dependent, but locally structured) events $B_Q$ should improve $3^{1/4}$ towards the empirical $1.7$.
* **Complete the index-eight theorem.** Prove that the caterpillar signature map is exactly eight-to-one for all $n$, i.e. $|\mathcal{C}_n| = n!/8$; equivalently, that a caterpillar is reconstructible from its quartet signature up to its automorphism group.
* **Characterise the tree code.** Give a complete list of local rules whose satisfaction characterises realisable ternary words — a "parity check matrix" for phylogenetic trees. On five leaves the rules cut $243$ words down to $15$; the general description is open.
* **Confirm $h(3) = 10$.** The bracket $10 \leq h(3) \leq h_{\mathrm{cat}}(3) \leq 6562$ should collapse; the restriction principle means that a single exhaustive verification at $n = 10$, if it can be organised within reach of computation, would settle it for all larger $n$.
* **Beyond quartets.** Replace "agreement on four leaves" by "agreement on $q$ leaves". The alphabet size becomes the number of binary trees on $q$ leaves, and the analogous balance theorem should follow from the same translation-by-transposition mechanism, giving lower bounds of the shape $h_q(k) > A_q^{\,(k-2)/q}$.

---

## 12. Conclusion

Encoding phylogenetic trees by their quartet resolutions places the common-quartet problem inside coding theory in a way that is faithful (agreement is exactly letter equality), exact (the three types are exactly equinumerous among caterpillars), and productive (a two-line first moment yields an exponential lower bound $h(k) > 3^{(k-2)/4}$). The same dictionary shows why the naive distance reading of the problem fails — over a ternary alphabet, full pairwise distance permits only three codewords — and exposes the local "parity check" structure that makes the realisable code a small, highly constrained subset of the ternary cube: $15$ words out of $243$ on five leaves, and at most $n!/8$ in general. On the upper side, a self-contained Erdős–Szekeres argument gives a doubly exponential bound, sharpened for two trees to the exact value $h_{\mathrm{cat}}(2) = 6$ by a restriction principle and a finite verification. What remains is the constant: the growth rate of $h(k)$ is a packing rate in a constrained ternary code, empirically near $1.7$, and pinning it down is the natural next problem.

\begin{abstract}
A fully resolved (binary) unrooted phylogenetic tree on a finite leaf set $X$ displays, on every four-element subset $Q\subseteq X$, exactly one of three resolutions. Encoding a tree by the vector of these resolutions embeds the set of trees on $n$ leaves into the ternary cube $\{0,1,2\}^{\binom{n}{4}}$, and under this embedding the statement ``the trees $T_1,\dots,T_k$ display a common quartet'' becomes ``the corresponding words carry a common letter in some coordinate''. \section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

An unrooted binary phylogenetic tree on a finite set $X$ of leaves is a tree whose leaves are bijectively labelled by $X$ and all of whose internal vertices have degree three. Such a tree is determined by its set of \emph{splits}: deleting an edge $e$ partitions $X$ into two nonempty blocks $A_e \mid X\setminus A_e$.

For $A\subseteq X$, the \emph{restriction} $T|_A$ is the tree on leaf set $A$ obtained by deleting all leaves outside $A$ and suppressing degree-two vertices; its split system consists of the sets $S\cap A$ for splits $S$ of $T$, keeping only nontrivial partitions of $A$.

For $|A|=4$, say $A=\{a,b,c,d\}$, a binary tree $T|_A$ has exactly one internal edge, hence exactly one nontrivial split, and there are exactly three possibilities:
\[
ab\mid cd,\qquad ac\mid bd,\qquad ad\mid bc .
\]
This restriction is the \emph{quartet displayed by $T$ on $A$}. Trees $T_1,\dots,T_k$ display a \emph{common quartet} on $A$ if all $T_i|_A$ coincide; equivalently, $A$ is a common agreement subtree of size four.

We call $n$ an \emph{agreement threshold for $k$ trees at size four} if every family of $k$ binary trees on a leaf set of size at least $n$ displays a common quartet on some four-element subset, and set
\[
h(k) := \min\{\, n : n \text{ is an agreement threshold for } k \text{ trees at size four} \,\}.
\]
The existence of $h(k)$ follows from the Ramsey-type argument of Section~\ref{sec:upper}. This paper concerns its growth rate.

We also write $h_{\mathrm{cat}}(k)$ for the same quantity with the trees restricted to \emph{caterpillars} (trees whose internal vertices lie on a single path). Caterpillars are binary trees, so $h_{\mathrm{cat}}(k)\le h(k)$ and all our lower bounds apply to $h$ itself; our upper bounds are proved for caterpillars and hence bound $h_{\mathrm{cat}}$. Every binary tree on at most five leaves is a caterpillar.

\subsection{The coding-theoretic reformulation}

Since the quartet displayed on a four-set is one of three possibilities, a tree $T$ on $n$ leaves determines a word
\[
\sigma(T)\in\{0,1,2\}^{\binom{X}{4}},
\]
its \emph{quartet signature}, whose $Q$-th letter records the resolution displayed on $Q$. Under this dictionary a four-set is a coordinate, agreement of a family on a four-set is constancy of the corresponding coordinate, and ``no common quartet'' becomes \emph{no constant coordinate}. Realisable signatures form a constrained subcode $\mathcal C_n \subseteq \{0,1,2\}^{\binom n4}$.

Two features drive the paper. First, the avoidance condition is a covering-type condition on the whole family, not a pairwise distance condition; Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} shows these are genuinely different and that the distance formulation is useless. Second, $\mathcal C_n$ is severely constrained by local rules on overlapping five-leaf subsets (Section~\ref{sec:structure}), the analogue of local parity checks, so the lower-bound argument must be carried out inside $\mathcal C_n$ --- which the caterpillar construction achieves.

\subsection{Summary of results}

Theorem~\ref{thm:balance} (exact ternary balance); Theorem~\ref{thm:firstmoment} and Corollary~\ref{cor:lower} (exponential lower bound $h(k) > 3^{(k-2)/4}$); Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} (distance collapse); Theorems~\ref{thm:five}, \ref{thm:packing} (code structure: $15=5!/8$ realisable five-leaf words; $8|\mathcal C_n|\le n!$); Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} ($h_{\mathrm{cat}}(2)=6$, $h(2)\ge 6$); Theorem~\ref{thm:family} and Theorem~\ref{thm:nine} ($10 \le h(3)$, $h_{\mathrm{cat}}(3)\le 6562$).

\section{Notation}

Throughout, $X$ is a finite leaf set, identified with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$; $S_n$ is the symmetric group. \emph{Types} $0,1,2$ refer to the pairings $ab|cd$, $ac|bd$, $ad|bc$ once an ordering $(a,b,c,d)$ of the four leaves is fixed. Permuting $(a,b,c,d)$ permutes the three types correspondingly, so agreement of two trees on a four-set is equivalent to equality of the types computed with respect to any single fixed ordering; the convention is harmless.

\section{Caterpillars and the ternary letter}

\subsection{Definition}

A \emph{caterpillar} is a binary tree all of whose internal vertices lie on a single path. Equivalently, a caterpillar on $n$ leaves is given by a linear order of the leaves: leaf $x$ is attached at position $\pi(x)$ along the backbone, $\pi\in S_n$; write $C_\pi$. Caterpillars are honest binary trees, so lower bounds proved for them apply to the general problem.

\begin{definition}\label{def:code3}
For four distinct natural numbers $p,q,r,s$ put
\[
\codethree(p,q,r,s) := \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } \max(p,q)<\min(r,s) \text{ or } \max(r,s)<\min(p,q),\\
1 & \text{else if } \max(p,r)<\min(q,s) \text{ or } \max(q,s)<\min(p,r),\\
2 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
and for a leaf order $\pi$ set $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d):=\codethree(\pi a,\pi b,\pi c,\pi d)$.
\end{definition}

On distinct arguments the three clauses are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, and the third admits the symmetric characterisation
\[
\codethree(p,q,r,s)=2 \iff \max(p,s)<\min(q,r) \text{ or } \max(q,r)<\min(p,s),
\]
so in all cases: \emph{the type is determined by which two of the four leaves occupy the two lowest positions}.

\begin{proposition}[The letter records the restricted tree]\label{prop:records}
Let $a,b,c,d$ be distinct leaves. Then $C_\pi|_{\{a,b,c,d\}}$ has nontrivial split $ab|cd$, $ac|bd$, $ad|bc$ according as $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)$ equals $0$, $1$, $2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The splits of $C_\pi$ are the backbone initial segments $A_j=\{x:\pi x<j\}$. A two-element subset $\{u,v\}\subseteq\{a,b,c,d\}$ arises as $A_j\cap\{a,b,c,d\}$ for some $j$ exactly when $u,v$ occupy the two lowest (equivalently, the two highest) positions among the four. Comparing with Definition~\ref{def:code3} gives the three equivalences.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Agreement forces letter equality]\label{cor:agree}
If $C_\pi$ and $C_\rho$ have equal restrictions to $\{a,b,c,d\}$, then $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)=\qc_\rho(a,b,c,d)$.
\end{corollary}

Thus the ternary letter is not a surrogate for the restricted tree: it \emph{is} the restricted tree.

\begin{proposition}[Order congruence]\label{prop:congr}
$\codethree(p,q,r,s)$ depends only on the relative order of its arguments: if the twelve order relations among $p,q,r,s$ agree with those among $p',q',r',s'$, then $\codethree(p,q,r,s)=\codethree(p',q',r',s')$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Restriction principle]\label{thm:restrict}
Let $\pi\in S_n$ and let $f:\{0,\dots,m-1\}\to\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ be injective. Then there is $\sigma\in S_m$ with
$\qc_\pi(fa,fb,fc,fd)=\qc_\sigma(a,b,c,d)$ for all $a,b,c,d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $g=\pi\circ f$ and let $\sigma(i)=|\{j: g(j)<g(i)\}|$ be the rank of $g(i)$. Ranking is a bijection onto $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ preserving all order relations, so Proposition~\ref{prop:congr} applies.
\end{proof}

\section{Exact ternary balance}

Let $Q_t(a,b,c,d):=\{\pi\in S_n : \qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)=t\}$.

\begin{lemma}[Transposition swaps two types]\label{lem:swap}
For distinct leaves $a,b,c,d$ and all $\pi\in S_n$,
\[
\qc_{\pi\circ(b\,c)}(a,b,c,d)=\tau_{01}\bigl(\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)\bigr),\qquad
\qc_{\pi\circ(b\,d)}(a,b,c,d)=\tau_{02}\bigl(\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)\bigr),
\]
where $\tau_{01}$ and $\tau_{02}$ are the transpositions $0\leftrightarrow 1$ and $0\leftrightarrow 2$ of types.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Precomposition with $(b\,c)$ exchanges the positions of $b$ and $c$ and fixes those of $a,d$. Substituting into Definition~\ref{def:code3} converts the clause characterising type $0$ into the clause characterising type $1$ and conversely, while the symmetric clause for type $2$ is invariant. The second identity is the same computation with $c$ and $d$ interchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:translate}
If $\tau\in S_n$ is an involution and $s$ a transposition of types with $\qc_{\pi\tau}=s(\qc_\pi)$ for all $\pi$, then $|Q_t|=|Q_{s(t)}|$ for every $t$. Consequently $|Q_0|=|Q_1|=|Q_2|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Exact ternary balance]\label{thm:balance}
For distinct leaves $a,b,c,d$ and each type $t$,
\[
3\cdot|Q_t(a,b,c,d)| = n! .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The three classes partition $S_n$ and are equinumerous by Lemmas~\ref{lem:swap} and \ref{lem:translate}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The theorem is exact, not asymptotic: a uniformly random caterpillar displays a prescribed type on four prescribed leaves with probability exactly $1/3$. It is a statement about the marginal distribution at one coordinate; different coordinates are far from independent, which is why only first moments are used below.
\end{remark}

\section{The first-moment lower bound}

Fix $k=m+1$ and regard $T=(T_0,\dots,T_m)\in S_n^{\,k}$ as an independent uniform sample.

\begin{lemma}[Agreement count]\label{lem:count}
For distinct leaves $a,b,c,d$, the number of families whose members all display the same type on $(a,b,c,d)$ equals $3\,|Q_0|^{\,k}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Partition according to the common type $t$; the fibre over $t$ is $Q_t^{\,k}$, of size $|Q_0|^k$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:balance}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact first moment]\label{lem:moment}
With $k=m+1$ one has $3^m\cdot 3\,|Q_0|^{\,k}=(n!)^{\,k}$; that is, $k$ independent uniform caterpillars agree on a fixed four-set with probability exactly $3^{-(k-1)}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[First-moment construction]\label{thm:firstmoment}
If $n^4<3^m$, there exist caterpillars $T_0,\dots,T_m$ on $n$ leaves such that for every quadruple $a,b,c,d$ of pairwise distinct leaves there are indices $i,j$ with $\qc_{T_i}(a,b,c,d)\ne \qc_{T_j}(a,b,c,d)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each ordered quadruple $Q$ of pairwise distinct leaves let $B_Q\subseteq S_n^{\,k}$ be the set of families agreeing on $Q$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:moment}, $3^m|B_Q|=(n!)^k$. There are at most $n^4$ such quadruples, so
\[
3^m\Bigl|\bigcup_Q B_Q\Bigr| \le \sum_Q 3^m|B_Q| \le n^4 (n!)^k < 3^m (n!)^k ,
\]
whence $|\bigcup_Q B_Q| < (n!)^k = |S_n^{\,k}|$. Any family outside the union has the stated property.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exponential lower bound]\label{cor:lower}
For every $v\ge 0$ there exist $4v+2$ binary trees on $3^v$ leaves with no common quartet; hence
\[
h(k) > 3^{\frac{k-2}{4}}\qquad (k\ge 2).
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take $n=3^v$, $m=4v+1$: then $n^4=3^{4v}<3^{4v+1}=3^m$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:firstmoment} yields $4v+2$ avoiding caterpillars, which by Corollary~\ref{cor:agree} have pairwise unequal restrictions on every four-set. Solving $k=4v+2$ for $v$ gives the bound.
\end{proof}

The certified rate is $3^{1/4}\approx 1.3161$ leaves per additional tree. Since Lemma~\ref{lem:moment} is an identity, the whole loss is in the union bound over $n^4$ quadruples.

\section{Why distance is the wrong invariant}

\begin{theorem}[Full-distance collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
Let $N\ge 1$ and let $\mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1,2\}^N$ be a family of words any two of which differ in \emph{every} coordinate. Then $|\mathcal F|\le 3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The map $w\mapsto w_1$ is injective on $\mathcal F$ and its codomain has three elements.
\end{proof}

The bound is attained by the three constant words and is independent of $N$. Hence a family of trees with pairwise maximum-distance signatures has at most three members, whereas Corollary~\ref{cor:lower} produces families of size growing linearly in $\log n$. The avoidance condition used there is strictly weaker --- in each coordinate \emph{some} pair disagrees, and the disagreeing pair may vary with the coordinate --- and it is exactly this many-body, covering-type condition that the first-moment method handles.

\section{Upper bounds}\label{sec:upper}

\begin{theorem}[Monotone subsets]\label{thm:es}
Let $f:\alpha\to\beta$ be injective, $\alpha$ a finite linearly ordered set and $\beta$ linearly ordered. If $|\alpha|>r^2$, there is $t\subseteq\alpha$ with $|t|>r$ on which $f$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $i\in\alpha$ let $u(i)$, $d(i)$ be the maximal lengths of increasing, resp.\ decreasing, chains ending at $i$. For $i<j$, injectivity forces $f(i)<f(j)$ or $f(j)<f(i)$, hence $u(i)<u(j)$ or $d(i)<d(j)$; so $i\mapsto(u(i),d(i))$ is injective. If all chains had length $\le r$ the image would lie in an $r\times r$ grid, contradicting $|\alpha|>r^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Monotone quadruples carry type $0$]\label{lem:mono}
If $a<b<c<d$ and $\pi$ is monotone on $\{a,b,c,d\}$, then $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)=0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Family upper bound]\label{thm:family}
Any $k$ caterpillars on more than $3^{2^k}$ leaves display a common quartet; indeed there are four distinct leaves on which all $k$ trees display the same type-$0$ resolution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Iterate Theorem~\ref{thm:es}: choose a subset on which the first order is monotone, inside it one on which the second is monotone, and so on. Each step takes size $N$ to roughly $\sqrt N$; after $k$ steps a starting size exceeding $3^{2^k}$ leaves at least four leaves on which every order is monotone. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}.
\end{proof}

Specialising to $k=2$ with $r=3$: any two caterpillars on at least $10$ leaves share a quartet. This is not sharp.

\begin{theorem}[Five leaves are not enough]\label{thm:fivetwo}
The caterpillars with leaf orders $(0,1,2,3,4)$ and $(0,3,2,1,4)$ display no common quartet: the first resolves all five of its quartets as type $0$, the second as $(2,1,1,1,2)$. Hence $h(2)\ge 6$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp two-tree bound]\label{thm:sharp}
Any two caterpillars on at least six leaves display a common quartet. Consequently $h_{\mathrm{cat}}(2)=6$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(a) \emph{Reduction}: by Theorem~\ref{thm:restrict}, restricting both orders along an injection from a six-element set yields two genuine six-leaf orders with the same letters, so a six-leaf obstruction transports upward. (b) \emph{Six leaves}: since $\qc_\pi(\sigma a,\sigma b,\sigma c,\sigma d)=\qc_{\pi\sigma}(a,b,c,d)$, comparing $(\pi,\rho)$ is equivalent, after right translation by $\pi^{-1}$, to comparing the identity order with $\rho\pi^{-1}$; an exhaustive check of the $720$ leaf orders against the identity confirms that a common quartet always exists, replacing $720^2=518400$ comparisons by $720$.
\end{proof}

Since every binary tree on at most five leaves is a caterpillar, Theorem~\ref{thm:fivetwo} gives the general lower bound as well.

\begin{theorem}[Nine leaves, three trees]\label{thm:nine}
The three leaf orders
\[
\mathrm{id},\qquad (7,0,2,5,4,3,1,8,6),\qquad (6,5,1,3,4,2,7,8,0)
\]
on nine leaves (listing the position of each of the leaves $0,\dots,8$) display no common quartet: on each of the $126$ four-element subsets at least two of the trees disagree.
\end{theorem}

Combining with Theorem~\ref{thm:family} for $k=3$, which requires more than $3^8=6561$ leaves,
\[
10\le h(3), \qquad h_{\mathrm{cat}}(3)\le 6562 .
\]

\section{Structure of the code}\label{sec:structure}

\subsection{Local consistency: the parity checks}

\begin{theorem}[Cherry propagation]\label{thm:cherry}
For any leaf order $\pi$ and leaves $a,b,c,d,e$: if $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)=0$ and $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,e)=0$, then $\qc_\pi(a,b,d,e)=0$. In words, $ab|cd$ and $ab|ce$ force $ab|de$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Type $0$ on $(a,b,c,d)$ says the positions of $a,b$ lie both below or both above those of $c,d$; likewise for $c,e$. Combining the inequalities places $a,b$ on one side of both $d$ and $e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forbidden configuration]
No leaf order displays $ab|cd$, $ab|ce$ and $ac|de$ simultaneously; the corresponding ternary word is not a codeword.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mixed rules]
For distinct leaves: $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)=0$ and $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,e)=1$ force $\qc_\pi(a,c,d,e)=2$; and $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,d)=0$ with $\qc_\pi(a,b,c,e)=2$ force $\qc_\pi(b,c,d,e)=2$.
\end{theorem}

All these rules follow by translating the type characterisations into linear inequalities among positions and eliminating. An exhaustive scan over the $120$ five-leaf orders and all premise pairs on overlapping quadruples yields $210$ valid two-premise implications of this kind, of which the above are representatives.

\subsection{The five-leaf code, counted exactly}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:five}
Exactly $15$ of the $3^5=243$ ternary words of length five arise as quartet signatures of five-leaf trees, and $8\cdot 15 = 120 = 5!$.
\end{theorem}

The five-leaf code rate is $\log_3(15)/5\approx 0.493$: less than half the ambient ternary dimension is used, so any packing bound computed in the unconstrained cube is far off. It matters that the argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:firstmoment} samples trees, hence lives inside the realisable code.

\subsection{Symmetries and the packing bound}

\begin{proposition}[Three symmetries]\label{prop:symm}
The quartet signature of a caterpillar is unchanged by (i) reversal of the leaf order, (ii) exchange of the two lowest positions, (iii) exchange of the two highest positions.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(i) Reversal $v\mapsto (n-1)-v$ flips every comparison at once, so all clauses of Definition~\ref{def:code3} are preserved, even for degenerate quadruples. (ii) Exchanging the values $0$ and $1$ preserves the type of every quadruple of distinct leaves, because the two swapped positions are the global minima and hence remain the ``low pair'' of any quadruple containing both; a case analysis over the remaining positions discharges the rest. (iii) is (ii) conjugated by (i).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Packing bound]\label{thm:packing}
For $n\ge 4$, the number $|\mathcal C_n|$ of distinct caterpillar quartet signatures satisfies $8\,|\mathcal C_n|\le n!$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $r$ be reversal, $a$ the exchange of the two lowest positions and $b=rar$. The eight products of $\{1,r\}\times\{1,a\}\times\{1,b\}$ are pairwise distinct for $n\ge 4$, as one sees by evaluating them at the first and last positions; by Proposition~\ref{prop:symm} every fibre of the signature map is a union of cosets of this group of order eight acting freely on $S_n$, hence has at least eight elements. Summing fibre sizes gives the bound.
\end{proof}

Exhaustive computation gives $|\mathcal C_n| = 3,15,90,630$ for $n=4,5,6,7$, i.e.\ exactly $n!/8$: the signature map is precisely eight-to-one. Equality for all $n$ is equivalent to reconstructibility of a caterpillar from its quartets up to its automorphisms, which we do not prove here.

\section{Algorithms and numerical results}

\paragraph{Computing a signature.} Iterate over the $\binom n4$ four-subsets and evaluate $\codethree$: $O(n^4)$ comparisons.

\paragraph{Verifying avoidance.} Compute the $k$ signatures and scan for a constant coordinate: $O(kn^4)$.

\paragraph{Group-reduced exhaustive search.} The identity $\qc_\pi(\sigma a,\sigma b,\sigma c,\sigma d)=\qc_{\pi\sigma}(a,b,c,d)$ reduces ``every pair of $n$-leaf caterpillars shares a quartet'' from $(n!)^2$ pairs to $n!$ orders compared against the identity; for $n=6$, $720$ instead of $518400$.

\paragraph{Local search.} Minimise $\mathrm{cost}(T_1,\dots,T_k):=\#\{Q: \text{all } T_i \text{ agree on } Q\}$ by randomised hill-climbing over transpositions of individual leaf orders with random restarts. Cost zero is an avoidance certificate; repeated failure is evidence, not proof, of nonexistence.

\section{Discussion}

The dictionary does three things. It makes agreement computable: agreement on a four-set is equality of a single letter, which is what makes exhaustive verification at $n=6$ and $n=9$ possible. It makes the first moment exact: by Theorem~\ref{thm:balance} the probability of $k$-fold agreement is exactly $3^{-(k-1)}$, so every inefficiency in Corollary~\ref{cor:lower} lies in the union bound. And it identifies the right notion of avoidance: Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} rules out the distance formulation decisively, leaving a covering-type condition read across the family.

Writing $h(k)=\Theta(c^k)$ for the conjectural shape of the answer, Corollary~\ref{cor:lower} gives $c\ge 3^{1/4}$ while the data suggest $c\approx 1.7$. In coding language $c$ is a \emph{packing rate in a constrained ternary code}: the supremum of rates at which words of $\mathcal C_n$ can be placed so that no coordinate is constant. Neither the constrained nature of $\mathcal C_n$ nor the many-body nature of the condition is captured by classical rate--distance theory.

The iterated Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres upper bound extracts a \emph{global} monotone pattern once per tree, squaring the required leaf number each time. But a common quartet is local: four leaves must line up, not a chain through the whole leaf set. The natural replacement is a Ramsey-type theorem for $4$-uniform hypergraphs with three colours, applied to the ternary colouring of $\binom{[n]}{4}$ induced by the family; this would plausibly replace $3^{2^k}$ by $c^k$.

\section{Future work}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Determine the rate.} Prove $h(k)\le Cc^k$ for an absolute $c$, closing the gap between $3^{(k-2)/4}$ and $3^{2^k}$, presumably by a Ramsey argument on $4$-uniform three-coloured hypergraphs exploiting the local rules of Section~\ref{sec:structure}.
\item \textbf{Sharpen the lower bound.} A local-lemma or entropy-compression treatment of the dependent events $B_Q$ should push $3^{1/4}$ towards the empirical $1.7$.
\item \textbf{Complete the index-eight theorem.} Show $|\mathcal C_n| = n!/8$ for all $n$: a caterpillar is reconstructible from its signature up to its automorphism group.
\item \textbf{Characterise the tree code.} Find a complete family of local rules characterising realisable words --- a ``parity check matrix'' for phylogenetic trees. On five leaves the rules cut $243$ words to $15$.
\item \textbf{Confirm $h(3)=10$.} The bracket $10\le h(3)\le h_{\mathrm{cat}}(3)\le 6562$ should collapse; by the restriction principle a single verification at $n=10$ settles all larger $n$.
\item \textbf{Beyond quartets.} Replace four by $q$ leaves; the alphabet becomes the set of binary trees on $q$ leaves, and the same translation-by-transposition mechanism should give $h_q(k) > A_q^{(k-2)/q}$.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

Encoding phylogenetic trees by their quartet resolutions places the common-quartet problem inside coding theory faithfully (agreement is exactly letter equality), exactly (the three types are exactly equinumerous among caterpillars) and productively (a short first-moment argument yields $h(k)>3^{(k-2)/4}$). The dictionary also explains why the naive distance reading fails --- over a ternary alphabet full pairwise distance permits only three codewords --- and exposes the local parity-check structure that makes the realisable code a small subset of the ternary cube: $15$ of $243$ on five leaves, at most $n!/8$ in general. On the upper side, Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres gives a doubly exponential bound, sharpened for two trees to $h_{\mathrm{cat}}(2)=6$ by a restriction principle and a finite verification. What remains is the constant: the growth rate of $h(k)$ is a packing rate in a constrained ternary code, empirically near $1.7$.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Order = Tuple[int, ...]  # order[leaf] = position of that leaf along the caterpillar
Quad = Tuple[int, int, int, int]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The ternary quartet letter
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def code3(p: int, q: int, r: int, s: int) -> int:
    """The quartet type of four distinct positions p, q, r, s on a path.

    Returns 0 for the pairing {1st,2nd}|{3rd,4th} of the argument list, i.e.
    ``pq|rs``; 1 for ``pr|qs``; 2 for ``ps|qr``.  On a caterpillar tree whose
    leaves hang off a path in the order given by the positions, two leaves are
    paired precisely when they occupy the two lowest (or the two highest)
    positions among the four.
    """
    if max(p, q) < min(r, s) or max(r, s) < min(p, q):
        return 0
    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):
        return 1
    return 2


def qcode(order: Order, a: int, b: int, c: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Quartet type displayed on leaves a,b,c,d by the caterpillar with `order`."""
    return code3(order[a], order[b], order[c], order[d])


def signature(order: Order, n: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Ternary word of length C(n,4): the quartet letters of the caterpillar."""
    return tuple(
        qcode(order, a, b, c, d) for a, b, c, d in itertools.combinations(range(n), 4)
    )


def all_orders(n: int) -> Iterable[Order]:
    return itertools.permutations(range(n))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact ternary balance
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def ternary_balance(n: int, quad: Quad) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Count the leaf orders on n leaves realising each type on a fixed quartet."""
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {0: 0, 1: 0, 2: 0}
    a, b, c, d = quad
    for order in all_orders(n):
        counts[qcode(order, a, b, c, d)] += 1
    return counts


def demo_balance() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2.  EXACT TERNARY BALANCE:  each type occurs for exactly n!/3 orders")
    print("=" * 74)
    for n, quad in ((4, (0, 1, 2, 3)), (5, (0, 2, 3, 4)), (6, (1, 2, 4, 5))):
        counts = ternary_balance(n, quad)
        total = sum(counts.values())
        fact = 1
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            fact *= i
        ok = all(3 * v == fact for v in counts.values())
        print(
            f"  n={n}, quartet {quad}:  counts {counts},  total {total} = {n}!"
            f"   balanced: {ok}"
        )
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. First moment and the exponential lower bound
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def agreement_probability(n: int, k: int, quad: Quad) -> Fraction:
    """Exact probability that k independent uniform leaf orders agree on `quad`."""
    counts = ternary_balance(n, quad)
    total = sum(counts.values())
    num = sum(v**k for v in counts.values())
    return Fraction(num, total**k)


def demo_first_moment() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The sharp two-tree threshold
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def common_quartets(orders: Sequence[Order], n: int) -> List[Quad]:
    """Quartets on which every caterpillar in the list displays the same type."""
    out: List[Quad] = []
    for quad in itertools.combinations(range(n), 4):
        a, b, c, d = quad
        t = qcode(orders[0], a, b, c, d)
        if all(qcode(o, a, b, c, d) == t for o in orders[1:]):
            out.append((a, b, c, d))
    return out


def compose(pi: Order, sigma: Order) -> Order:
    """Composition (pi o sigma) of two permutations given in one-line notation."""
    return tuple(pi[sigma[i]] for i in range(len(sigma)))


def inverse(pi: Order) -> Order:
    out = [0] * len(pi)
    for i, v in enumerate(pi):
        out[v] = i
    return tuple(out)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Full Hamming distance collapses over a ternary alphabet
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def largest_full_distance_family(length: int, alphabet: int = 3) -> int:
    """Largest family of words pairwise differing in EVERY coordinate."""
    best = 0
    words = list(itertools.product(range(alphabet), repeat=length))

    def extend(chosen: List[Tuple[int, ...]], start: int) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        best = max(best, len(chosen))
        for i in range(start, len(words)):
            w = words[i]
            if all(all(x != y for x, y in zip(w, c)) for c in chosen):
                chosen.append(w)
                extend(chosen, i + 1)
                chosen.pop()

    extend([], 0)
    return best


def demo_distance_collapse() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8.  FULL-DISTANCE FAMILIES OVER A TERNARY ALPHABET HAVE <= 3 MEMBERS")
    print("=" * 74)
    for length in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        print(f"  word length {length}: largest family = {largest_full_distance_family(length)}")
    print("  Reason: the first letters are pairwise distinct, and there are only three.")
    print("  So 'no common quartet' cannot be obtained by maximising Hamming distance;")
    print("  the correct notion is the weaker 'no constant coordinate'.")
    print()

def type_vector(order: Order, quads: Sequence[Quad]) -> List[int]:
    return [code3(order[a], order[b], order[c], order[d]) for a, b, c, d in quads]


def agreement_cost(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Number of coordinates on which all words carry the same letter."""
    first = vectors[0]
    total = 0
    for idx, t in enumerate(first):
        if all(v[idx] == t for v in vectors[1:]):
            total += 1
    return total

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Order = Tuple[int, ...]  # order[leaf] = position of that leaf along the caterpillar
Quad = Tuple[int, int, int, int]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The ternary quartet letter
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def code3(p: int, q: int, r: int, s: int) -> int:
    """The quartet type of four distinct positions p, q, r, s on a path.

    Returns 0 for the pairing {1st,2nd}|{3rd,4th} of the argument list, i.e.
    ``pq|rs``; 1 for ``pr|qs``; 2 for ``ps|qr``.  On a caterpillar tree whose
    leaves hang off a path in the order given by the positions, two leaves are
    paired precisely when they occupy the two lowest (or the two highest)
    positions among the four.
    """
    if max(p, q) < min(r, s) or max(r, s) < min(p, q):
        return 0
    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):
        return 1
    return 2


def qcode(order: Order, a: int, b: int, c: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Quartet type displayed on leaves a,b,c,d by the caterpillar with `order`."""
    return code3(order[a], order[b], order[c], order[d])


def signature(order: Order, n: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Ternary word of length C(n,4): the quartet letters of the caterpillar."""
    return tuple(
        qcode(order, a, b, c, d) for a, b, c, d in itertools.combinations(range(n), 4)
    )


def all_orders(n: int) -> Iterable[Order]:
    return itertools.permutations(range(n))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact ternary balance
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def ternary_balance(n: int, quad: Quad) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Count the leaf orders on n leaves realising each type on a fixed quartet."""
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {0: 0, 1: 0, 2: 0}
    a, b, c, d = quad
    for order in all_orders(n):
        counts[qcode(order, a, b, c, d)] += 1
    return counts


def demo_balance() -> None:

        fact = 1
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            fact *= i
        ok = all(3 * v == fact for v in counts.values())
        print(
            f"  n={n}, quartet {quad}:  counts {counts},  total {total} = {n}!"
            f"   balanced: {ok}"
        )
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. First moment and the exponential lower bound
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def agreement_probability(n: int, k: int, quad: Quad) -> Fraction:
    """Exact probability that k independent uniform leaf orders agree on `quad`."""
    counts = ternary_balance(n, quad)
    total = sum(counts.values())
    num = sum(v**k for v in counts.values())
    return Fraction(num, total**k)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The sharp two-tree threshold
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def common_quartets(orders: Sequence[Order], n: int) -> List[Quad]:
    """Quartets on which every caterpillar in the list displays the same type."""
    out: List[Quad] = []
    for quad in itertools.combinations(range(n), 4):
        a, b, c, d = quad
        t = qcode(orders[0], a, b, c, d)
        if all(qcode(o, a, b, c, d) == t for o in orders[1:]):
            out.append((a, b, c, d))
    return out


def compose(pi: Order, sigma: Order) -> Order:
    """Composition (pi o sigma) of two permutations given in one-line notation."""
    return tuple(pi[sigma[i]] for i in range(len(sigma)))


def inverse(pi: Order) -> Order:
    out = [0] * len(pi)
    for i, v in enumerate(pi):
        out[v] = i
    return tuple(out)

def largest_full_distance_family(length: int, alphabet: int = 3) -> int:
    """Largest family of words pairwise differing in EVERY coordinate."""
    best = 0
    words = list(itertools.product(range(alphabet), repeat=length))

    def extend(chosen: List[Tuple[int, ...]], start: int) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        best = max(best, len(chosen))
        for i in range(start, len(words)):
            w = words[i]
            if all(all(x != y for x, y in zip(w, c)) for c in chosen):
                chosen.append(w)
                extend(chosen, i + 1)
                chosen.pop()

    extend([], 0)
    return best

    print("8.  FULL-DISTANCE FAMILIES OVER A TERNARY ALPHABET HAVE <= 3 MEMBERS")
    print("=" * 74)

        print(f"  word length {length}: largest family = {largest_full_distance_family(length)}")
    print("  Reason: the first letters are pairwise distinct, and there are only three.")
    print("  So 'no common quartet' cannot be obtained by maximising Hamming distance;")
    print("  the correct notion is the weaker 'no constant coordinate'.")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. How large can an avoiding family be?  A randomised search
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def type_vector(order: Order, quads: Sequence[Quad]) -> List[int]:
    return [code3(order[a], order[b], order[c], order[d]) for a, b, c, d in quads]


def agreement_cost(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Number of coordinates on which all words carry the same letter."""
    first = vectors[0]
    total = 0
    for idx, t in enumerate(first):
        if all(v[idx] == t for v in vectors[1:]):
            total += 1
    return total


def search_avoiding(k: int, n: int, restarts: int = 3, steps: int = 600,
                    seed: int = 20240825) -> Sequence[Order] | None:
    """Local search for k leaf orders on n leaves with no common quartet."""
    rng = random.Random(seed + 1000 * k + n)
    quads = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 4))
    for _ in range(restarts):
        orders: List[Order] = []
        for _ in range(k):
            p = list(range(n))
            rng.shuffle(p)
            orders.append(tuple(p))
        vectors = [type_vector(o, quads) for o in orders]
        cur = agreement_cost(vectors)
        for _ in range(steps):
            if cur == 0:
                return orders
            i = rng.randrange(k)
            p = list(orders[i])
            x, y = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
            p[x], p[y] = p[y], p[x]
            cand = tuple(p)
            cand_vec = type_vector(cand, quads)
            old_vec = vectors[i]
            vectors[i] = cand_vec
            new = agreement_cost(vectors)
            if new <= cur:
                orders[i], cur = cand, new
            else:
                vectors[i] = old_vec
        if cur == 0:
            return orders
    return None


def demo_search() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("9.  EMPIRICAL GROWTH OF THE LARGEST AVOIDING LEAF NUMBER")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("  (local search; a failure is evidence, not proof, that none exists)")

        for n in range(4, 19):

            if found is not None:

        record[k] = best
        print(f"  {k:>8} {best:>44}")
    ks = sorted(record)

                f"  ratio n(k={k2})/n(k={k1}) = {record[k2] / record[k1]:.2f}"
                f"   (certified rate from the first moment: 3^(1/4) = 1.32)"
            )
    print()

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Iterator, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Order = Tuple[int, ...]
Quad = Tuple[int, int, int, int]


def code3(p: int, q: int, r: int, s: int) -> int:
    """Ternary quartet letter of four distinct backbone positions."""
    if max(p, q) < min(r, s) or max(r, s) < min(p, q):
        return 0
    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):
        return 1
    return 2


def quads(n: int) -> List[Quad]:
    return list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 4))  # type: ignore[arg-type]


def common_quartets(orders: Sequence[Order], n: int) -> List[Quad]:
    out: List[Quad] = []
    for a, b, c, d in quads(n):
        t = code3(orders[0][a], orders[0][b], orders[0][c], orders[0][d])
        if all(code3(o[a], o[b], o[c], o[d]) == t for o in orders[1:]):
            out.append((a, b, c, d))
    return out


def shares_with_identity(u: Order, n: int) -> Optional[Quad]:
    ident = tuple(range(n))
    for a, b, c, d in quads(n):
        if code3(ident[a], ident[b], ident[c], ident[d]) == code3(u[a], u[b], u[c], u[d]):
            return (a, b, c, d)
    return None

def code3(p: int, q: int, r: int, s: int) -> int:
    """Ternary quartet letter of four distinct backbone positions.

    Returns 0 for the resolution pairing the 1st with the 2nd argument
    (``pq|rs``), 1 for ``pr|qs`` and 2 for ``ps|qr``.  The rule is: the two
    leaves occupying the two lowest positions among the four are the ones that

    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):

    return 2

import itertools
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Order = Tuple[int, ...]


def code3(p: int, q: int, r: int, s: int) -> int:
    if max(p, q) < min(r, s) or max(r, s) < min(p, q):
        return 0
    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):
        return 1
    return 2


def compose(pi: Order, sigma: Order) -> Order:
    """(pi o sigma)(i) = pi[sigma[i]], for permutations in one-line notation."""
    return tuple(pi[sigma[i]] for i in range(len(sigma)))


def inverse(pi: Order) -> Order:
    out = [0] * len(pi)
    for i, v in enumerate(pi):
        out[v] = i
    return tuple(out)


def shares_quartet_with_identity(u: Order, n: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int, int]]:
    """Return a four-set on which `u` and the identity order agree, if any.

    Because the quartet letter satisfies  q_pi(sigma a, ..., sigma d)
    = q_{pi o sigma}(a, ..., d), a pair (pi, rho) shares a quartet if and only
    if the identity order shares one with rho o pi^{-1}.  This reduces an
    (n!)^2 verification to n! single comparisons.
    """
    ident = tuple(range(n))
    for a, b, c, d in itertools.combinations(range(n), 4):
        if code3(ident[a], ident[b], ident[c], ident[d]) == code3(u[a], u[b], u[c], u[d]):
            return (a, b, c, d)
    return None


def pair_threshold_holds(n: int) -> bool:
    """True iff every pair of caterpillars on n leaves shares a quartet."""
    return all(
        shares_quartet_with_identity(u, n) is not None
        for u in itertools.permutations(range(n))
    )

    """All orders sharing no quartet with the identity (avoidance witnesses)."""
    return [
        u
        for u in itertools.permutations(range(n))
        if shares_quartet_with_identity(u, n) is None
    ]

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import random
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Order = Tuple[int, ...]
Quad = Tuple[int, int, int, int]


def code3(p: int, q: int, r: int, s: int) -> int:
    if max(p, q) < min(r, s) or max(r, s) < min(p, q):
        return 0
    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):
        return 1
    return 2


def type_vector(order: Order, quads: Sequence[Quad]) -> List[int]:
    return [code3(order[a], order[b], order[c], order[d]) for a, b, c, d in quads]


def agreement_count(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Number of coordinates carrying the same letter in every word."""
    head = vectors[0]
    return sum(
        1 for i, t in enumerate(head) if all(v[i] == t for v in vectors[1:])
    )


def first_moment_size(n: int) -> int:
    """Least family size k = m+1 for which the union bound n^4 < 3^m applies."""
    m = 0
    while 3**m <= n**4:
        m += 1
    return m + 1


def sample_avoiding_family(n: int, k: int, tries: int = 5000,
                           seed: int = 0) -> Optional[List[Order]]:
    """Rejection sampling: draw k uniform leaf orders until none agree."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    quads = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 4))
    base = list(range(n))
    for _ in range(tries):
        family: List[Order] = []
        for _ in range(k):
            rng.shuffle(base)
            family.append(tuple(base))
        if agreement_count([type_vector(o, quads) for o in family]) == 0:
            return family
    return None


def local_search_avoiding(n: int, k: int, restarts: int = 4, steps: int = 1500,
                          seed: int = 0) -> Optional[List[Order]]:
    """Hill-climb on the number of agreeing four-sets; 0 is a certificate."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    quads = list(itertools.combinations(range(n), 4))
    for _ in range(restarts):
        family: List[Order] = []
        for _ in range(k):
            p = list(range(n))
            rng.shuffle(p)
            family.append(tuple(p))
        vectors = [type_vector(o, quads) for o in family]
        cur = agreement_count(vectors)
        for _ in range(steps):
            if cur == 0:
                return family
            i = rng.randrange(k)
            p = list(family[i])
            x, y = rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(n)
            p[x], p[y] = p[y], p[x]
            cand = tuple(p)
            old = vectors[i]
            vectors[i] = type_vector(cand, quads)
            new = agreement_count(vectors)
            if new <= cur:
                family[i], cur = cand, new
            else:
                vectors[i] = old
        if cur == 0:
            return family
    return None

    if max(p, q) < min(r, s) or max(r, s) < min(p, q):

    if max(p, r) < min(q, s) or max(q, s) < min(p, r):

    return 2


def canonical(a: int, b: int, c: int, d: int) -> Tuple[Quad, Dict[int, int]]:
    """Sort the four leaves and record how the three types are relabelled."""
    order = sorted([a, b, c, d])
    pairs = {
        0: frozenset({a, b}),
        1: frozenset({a, c}),
        2: frozenset({a, d}),
    }
    w, x, y, z = order
    canon = {
        frozenset({w, x}): 0,
        frozenset({w, y}): 1,
        frozenset({w, z}): 2,
    }
    relabel: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for t, pair in pairs.items():
        if pair in canon:
            relabel[t] = canon[pair]
        else:  # the complementary pair defines the same split
            comp = frozenset({w, x, y, z} - pair)
            relabel[t] = canon[comp]
    return (w, x, y, z), relabel

    """The type of the four leaves in the given order, read from a word."""
    quad, relabel = canonical(a, b, c, d)
    inverse = {v: k for k, v in relabel.items()}
    return inverse[word[quad]]

  "interactive_layout": "# Quartet Codes — a guided tour

*From "which four species go together?" to an exponential lower bound, in nine steps.*

---

## 1. Three stories about four species

Take four species and ask how they are related. A fully resolved evolutionary tree on four labelled
tips always splits them $2+2$, and there are exactly three ways to do it:

$$ab|cd, \qquad ac|bd, \qquad ad|bc.$$

There is no fourth option and no way to abstain. That little "three" is the seed of everything on this
page.

A large tree contains an enormous number of small ones: from a tree on $n$ species you can read off a
quartet for each of the $\binom{n}{4}$ four-element subsets, by deleting the other species and tidying
up. Collect all those answers and you have written the tree down as a **word over a three-letter
alphabet**, one letter per four-element subset. We call it the tree's *quartet signature*.

Now the question we care about. Real data give many trees for the same species — one per gene, one per
laboratory — and the practical question is what they agree on. The cleanest form of agreement is a
**common quartet**: four species that every tree resolves the same way.

> **The problem.** Let $h(k)$ be the smallest number of species that forces *any* $k$ fully resolved
> trees to display a common quartet. How fast does $h(k)$ grow?

<details>
<summary>Why the quartet signature determines the tree (background)</summary>

A tree on leaf set $X$ is determined by its **splits**: cutting an edge partitions $X$ into two blocks.
Restricting to a four-element subset $A$ leaves a tree with exactly one internal edge, hence exactly one
nontrivial split of $A$ — the quartet. Classical phylogenetics shows that the whole collection of
quartets recovers the tree, so nothing is lost in passing to the signature. What we gain is that
"agreement on four species" turns into the completely mechanical condition "these two words carry the
same letter in this coordinate". Further reading:
[phylogenetic tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetic_tree),
[quartet method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartet_distance).
</details>

---

## 2. Play first: hunt for trees that agree on nothing

Here is the whole problem in one picture. Each row below is a tree; each column is a four-species set;
each cell is coloured by the resolution that tree displays there. A **red-boxed column** is a column in
which every tree carries the same colour — a common quartet. Your goal: rearrange the trees until no
red boxes remain.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Try this sequence:

1. Set 5 species, 2 trees, press *reset to identity*: every column is red — identical trees agree

2. Now click species **B** and then **D** in the second row. All red boxes vanish. Two trees on five

3. Raise the species count to 6, still 2 trees, and press *hunt* as often as you like. It never works.
   **Six species always force two backbone trees to agree somewhere**: this is the exact value $h(2)=6$ for
   this class of trees.
4. Go to 9 species and 3 trees and press *hunt*. It succeeds — three trees on nine species can agree on
   nothing, so $h(3)\ge 10$.

## 3. Caterpillars: trees you can shuffle like a deck of cards

To do probability with trees we need trees that are easy to randomise. The simplest fully resolved
trees are the **caterpillars**: one long backbone with species hanging off it one at a time. A
caterpillar is nothing but an ordering of the species, so a random caterpillar is a shuffled deck.

Their quartet rule is as simple as it can be: among the four species, the two that sit **lowest** along
the backbone pair up, and so do the two highest.

<details>
<summary>The rule in symbols (click to reveal)</summary>

For four distinct backbone positions $p,q,r,s$ define

$$\mathrm{code}_3(p,q,r,s) = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } \max(p,q) < \min(r,s) \text{ or } \max(r,s) < \min(p,q),\\
1 & \text{else if } \max(p,r) < \min(q,s) \text{ or } \max(q,s) < \min(p,r),\\
2 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}$$

On distinct arguments the third case has the same symmetric shape as the first two:
$\mathrm{code}_3 = 2$ exactly when $\max(p,s) < \min(q,r)$ or $\max(q,r) < \min(p,s)$. Two consequences
matter later: the letter depends only on the *relative order* of the four positions (so deleting other
species never changes it), and exchanging two of the four positions *permutes* the three letters.
</details>

The algorithm that turns an ordering into a word is the primitive behind every computation on this
page:

## 4. One third, exactly

Here is the first theorem, and the reason the whole argument works without error terms.

> **Ternary balance.** Fix four distinct species. Of the $n!$ caterpillars on $n$ species, exactly
> $n!/3$ display each of the three quartet types on those four.

Turn the dials in the machine below and watch the three columns come out level, every single time.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary>The proof in three sentences (click to reveal)</summary>

Exchange the backbone places of the second and third of the four chosen species. This is an involution
of the set of all orderings, hence a bijection, and inspection of the inequalities shows that it turns
type $0$ into type $1$ and back, while fixing type $2$. Exchanging the second and fourth species does
the same for types $0$ and $2$. Three classes that are pairwise equinumerous and partition all $n!$
orderings must each have exactly $n!/3$ members.
</details>

The consequence is an exact probability: $k$ independent random caterpillars display the *same* quartet
on four fixed species with probability exactly

$$3 \cdot \left(\tfrac13\right)^{k} = 3^{-(k-1)}.$$

Panel 2 of the machine above lets you slide $k$ and $n$ and watch the expected number of common
quartets, $\binom{n}{4} 3^{-(k-1)}$, drop below $1$.

## 5. The exponential lower bound

Once the expected number of agreeing coordinates is below one, some outcome of the random experiment
must have **zero** of them. That is the whole proof.

> **Theorem.** If $n^4 < 3^m$, there exist $m+1$ trees on $n$ species with no common quartet. Taking
> $n = 3^v$ and $m = 4v+1$: some $4v+2$ trees on $3^v$ species agree on nothing, so
> $$h(k) > 3^{(k-2)/4}.$$

Each additional tree buys a factor $3^{1/4} \approx 1.316$ in species. The construction is
non-explicit, but explicit families are easy to find by search — and they are much better than the
counting bound guarantees:

## 7. The trap: distance is the wrong idea

A coding theorist's reflex is to build such families by maximising Hamming distance: demand that any
two words differ in *every* coordinate. Panel 3 of the balance machine above lets you test this — and
it fails spectacularly.

> **Collapse theorem.** Over a three-letter alphabet, a family of words that pairwise differ in every
> coordinate has at most **three** members, no matter how long the words are.

*Proof.* Look at the first letter of each word: any two differ there, and there are only three possible
first letters. $\square$

So the correct condition is genuinely weaker and genuinely many-body: **in each coordinate, somebody
disagrees** — not everybody, and possibly a different pair in each coordinate. This is a covering-type
condition across the family, not a pairwise packing condition, and it is exactly what the first-moment
argument delivers.

---

## 8. The code has parity checks

Not every ternary word is a tree. Signatures obey local rules involving five species at a time — the
analogue of parity checks in a linear code.

* **Cherry propagation.** $ab|cd$ and $ab|ce$ force $ab|de$: once $a$ and $b$ are joined at one end,
  they stay joined.
* **Forbidden configuration.** Consequently no tree displays $ab|cd$, $ab|ce$ and $ad|be$ together.
* **Mixed rules.** $ab|cd$ with $ac|be$ forces $ae|cd$; $ab|cd$ with $ae|bc$ forces $be|cd$.

How much do these cut down? On five species the ambient cube has $3^5 = 243$ words. Cherry propagation
alone eliminates all but $21$ of them, and the true code has exactly $15$ members — a rate of
$\log_3(15)/5 \approx 0.49$.

{{algorithm:3}}

The number $15$ is $5!/8$, and the $8$ has a geometric meaning: reading a caterpillar backwards gives
the same tree, and so does swapping the two species at either end (they form a cherry, and cherries
have no internal order). Those three moves generate a group of order eight acting freely, so the number
of distinct signatures is at most $n!/8$; computation confirms equality for $n = 4,5,6,7$, where the
counts are $3, 15, 90, 630$.

---

## 9. The ceiling, and the gap that remains

What forces agreement? For two trees, the [Erdős–Szekeres
theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Szekeres_theorem) does the job: any injective
sequence of more than $9$ terms has a monotone subsequence of length four, and four species ordered the
same way (or exactly oppositely) by both trees necessarily carry the same quartet. So ten species
suffice — but ten is not the truth. Because the quartet letter depends only on relative order, a
six-species obstruction, once verified, propagates to every larger species set; and the six-species
verification succeeds. Hence $h(2)=6$ exactly for backbone-shaped trees, and $h(2)\ge 6$ in general.

The following algorithm is what makes that verification cheap: instead of all $720^2 = 518400$ pairs it
checks $720$ single orderings against the identity, using the identity
$\mathrm{q}_\pi(\sigma a,\sigma b,\sigma c,\sigma d) = \mathrm{q}_{\pi\sigma}(a,b,c,d)$.

{{algorithm:1}}

Iterating the extraction across $k$ trees gives an upper bound too — more than $3^{2^k}$ species force
$k$ trees to agree — but that is *doubly* exponential, and for three trees it yields only

## Where this leaves the problem

The dictionary between trees and ternary words is faithful (agreement *is* letter equality), exact (the
three types are *exactly* equinumerous), and productive (a two-line first moment gives an exponential
lower bound). What remains is the constant: the growth rate of $h(k)$ is a **packing rate in a
constrained ternary code** — the largest rate at which one can place codewords of the tree code so that
no coordinate is ever constant. It lies between $3^{1/4} \approx 1.32$ and $2$, empirically near $1.7$,
and pinning it down is the natural next problem. The likely route: replace the wasteful global
monotone-pattern extraction by a Ramsey-type theorem for $4$-uniform hypergraphs with three colours,
applied directly to the ternary colouring of $\binom{[n]}{4}$ that a family of trees induces.

namespace QuartetCodes

section IndexEight

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- Exchange of the two smallest values. -/
def sw01 (x : ℕ) : ℕ := if x = 0 then 1 else if x = 1 then 0 else x

/-- Exchanging the two smallest positions does not change the quartet type of four distinct

    code3 (sw01 p) (sw01 q) (sw01 r) (sw01 s) = code3 p q r s := by
  unfold code3 sw01
  split_ifs <;> first | rfl | (exfalso; omega)

/-- Whether the four entries of a quadruple are pairwise distinct. -/
def QuadDistinct (q : Fin n × Fin n × Fin n × Fin n) : Prop :=
  q.1 ≠ q.2.1 ∧ q.1 ≠ q.2.2.1 ∧ q.1 ≠ q.2.2.2 ∧ q.2.1 ≠ q.2.2.1 ∧ q.2.1 ≠ q.2.2.2 ∧

      have hv1 : v.val ≠ 1 := fun h => h1 (Fin.ext h)

Tree-realisable quartet signatures form a *constrained* subcode; the constraints are local (they

open Finset

namespace QuartetCodes

section LocalRules

variable {n : ℕ} {π : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)} {a b c d e : Fin n}

/-- **Cherry propagation.**  If the leaves `a b` are separated from `c d` and from `c e`, they are
separated from `d e` as well. -/
theorem qcode_zero_trans (h1 : qcode π a b c d = 0) (h2 : qcode π a b c e = 0) :
    qcode π a b d e = 0 := by
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_zero_iff] at h1 h2 ⊢
  omega

/-- A five-leaf rule mixing the types `0` and `1`. -/
theorem qcode_zero_one_rule (hac : a ≠ c) (had : a ≠ d) (hae : a ≠ e)
    (hcd : c ≠ d) (hce : c ≠ e) (hde : d ≠ e)
    (h1 : qcode π a b c d = 0) (h2 : qcode π a b c e = 1) :
    qcode π a c d e = 2 := by
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_zero_iff] at h1
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_one_iff] at h2
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_two_iff (perm_val_ne hac) (perm_val_ne had) (perm_val_ne hae)
    (perm_val_ne hcd) (perm_val_ne hce) (perm_val_ne hde)]
  omega

/-- A five-leaf rule mixing the types `0` and `2`. -/
theorem qcode_zero_two_rule (hab : a ≠ b) (hac : a ≠ c) (hae : a ≠ e) (hbc : b ≠ c)
    (hbd : b ≠ d) (hbe : b ≠ e) (hcd : c ≠ d) (hce : c ≠ e) (hde : d ≠ e)
    (h1 : qcode π a b c d = 0) (h2 : qcode π a b c e = 2) :
    qcode π b c d e = 2 := by
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_zero_iff] at h1
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_two_iff (perm_val_ne hab) (perm_val_ne hac) (perm_val_ne hae)
    (perm_val_ne hbc) (perm_val_ne hbe) (perm_val_ne hce)] at h2
  rw [qcode, code3_eq_two_iff (perm_val_ne hbc) (perm_val_ne hbd) (perm_val_ne hbe)
    (perm_val_ne hcd) (perm_val_ne hce) (perm_val_ne hde)]
  omega

theorem qcode_forbidden (h1 : qcode π a b c d = 0) (h2 : qcode π a b c e = 0) :
    qcode π a b d e ≠ 1 := by
  rw [qcode_zero_trans h1 h2]

end LocalRules

/-- The five quadruples of a five-leaf set, as ordered tuples. -/

(increasing or decreasing) subset of size four.  Combined with the observation that a quadruple of
leaves ordered the same way — or in exactly opposite ways — by two caterpillars carries the same
quartet type, this yields the upper bound.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
Since the first-moment bound needs `n^4 < 3^m`, it is vacuous for two trees (`m = 1`).  Conjecture:
for two trees a *constant* number of leaves already forces a common quartet, and Erdős–Szekeres
supplies the constant.

## Experiment (Experimenter)
Exhaustive search over all `120^2` pairs of leaf orders on five leaves found pairs with no common
quartet; over all pairs on six leaves none exists (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`).  So the true
threshold for two caterpillars is `6`; Erdős–Szekeres with `r = s = 3` proves `10`, and the
five-leaf pair `not_isAgreementThreshold_five_two` shows the truth is at least `6`.

## Analysis (Analyst)
The gap `6 ≤ h_cat(2) ≤ 10` isolates exactly what the monotone-subsequence argument loses: it
insists on a quadruple that is monotone, whereas a common quartet only needs the *unordered*
`2 + 2` split to coincide.

## Critique (Critic)
The upper bound is proved for caterpillars (leaf orders), the same class in which the lower bound
constructs its avoiding families, so the two bounds are comparable.  Nothing here is proved by
`decide` on the whole statement: the Erdős–Szekeres step is a genuine pigeonhole over the pair
`(longest increasing chain, longest decreasing chain)`.
-/

open Finset

namespace QuartetCodes

/-! ## Erdős–Szekeres, self-contained -/

section ErdosSzekeres

variable {α β : Type*} [LinearOrder α] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [LinearOrder β]

/-- `t` is a strictly increasing chain for `f`. -/
def IsIncChain (f : α → β) (t : Finset α) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ t, ∀ y ∈ t, x < y → f x < f y

/-- `t` is a strictly decreasing chain for `f`. -/
def IsDecChain (f : α → β) (t : Finset α) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ t, ∀ y ∈ t, x < y → f y < f x

instance (f : α → β) (t : Finset α) : Decidable (IsIncChain f t) := by
  unfold IsIncChain; infer_instance

instance (f : α → β) (t : Finset α) : Decidable (IsDecChain f t) := by
  unfold IsDecChain; infer_instance

/-- The increasing chains ending at `i`. -/
def incChainsTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : Finset (Finset α) :=
  {t : Finset α | IsIncChain f t ∧ i ∈ t ∧ ∀ j ∈ t, j ≤ i}

/-- The decreasing chains ending at `i`. -/
def decChainsTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : Finset (Finset α) :=
  {t : Finset α | IsDecChain f t ∧ i ∈ t ∧ ∀ j ∈ t, j ≤ i}

/-- Length of the longest increasing chain ending at `i`. -/
def incTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : ℕ := (incChainsTo f i).sup Finset.card

/-- Length of the longest decreasing chain ending at `i`. -/
def decTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : ℕ := (decChainsTo f i).sup Finset.card

lemma singleton_mem_incChainsTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : ({i} : Finset α) ∈ incChainsTo f i := by
  simp only [incChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
  refine ⟨?_, by simp, ?_⟩
  · intro x hx y hy hxy
    simp only [Finset.mem_singleton] at hx hy
    exact absurd (hx.trans hy.symm) (ne_of_lt hxy)
  · intro j hj; simp only [Finset.mem_singleton] at hj; exact le_of_eq hj

lemma singleton_mem_decChainsTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : ({i} : Finset α) ∈ decChainsTo f i := by
  simp only [decChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
  refine ⟨?_, by simp, ?_⟩
  · intro x hx y hy hxy
    simp only [Finset.mem_singleton] at hx hy
    exact absurd (hx.trans hy.symm) (ne_of_lt hxy)
  · intro j hj; simp only [Finset.mem_singleton] at hj; exact le_of_eq hj

lemma one_le_incTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : 1 ≤ incTo f i := by
  have h : ({i} : Finset α).card ≤ incTo f i :=
    Finset.le_sup (f := Finset.card) (singleton_mem_incChainsTo f i)
  rwa [Finset.card_singleton] at h

lemma one_le_decTo (f : α → β) (i : α) : 1 ≤ decTo f i := by
  have h : ({i} : Finset α).card ≤ decTo f i :=
    Finset.le_sup (f := Finset.card) (singleton_mem_decChainsTo f i)
  rwa [Finset.card_singleton] at h

/-- An increasing step strictly increases the longest increasing chain length. -/
lemma incTo_lt_incTo {f : α → β} {i j : α} (hij : i < j) (hf : f i < f j) :
    incTo f i < incTo f j := by
  obtain ⟨t, ht, hsup⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_mem_eq_sup (incChainsTo f i) ⟨{i}, singleton_mem_incChainsTo f i⟩ Finset.card
  simp only [incChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at ht
  obtain ⟨hchain, hmem, hle⟩ := ht
  have hjt : j ∉ t := fun hj => absurd (hle j hj) (not_le.2 hij)
  have hnew : insert j t ∈ incChainsTo f j := by
    simp only [incChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
    refine ⟨?_, Finset.mem_insert_self _ _, ?_⟩
    · intro x hx y hy hxy
      rcases Finset.mem_insert.1 hx with rfl | hx' <;> rcases Finset.mem_insert.1 hy with rfl | hy'
      · exact absurd rfl (ne_of_lt hxy)
      · exact absurd (hle y hy') (not_le.2 (lt_trans hij hxy))
      · -- `x ∈ t`, `y = j`
        have hxi : x ≤ i := hle x hx'
        rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hxi with rfl | hlt
        · exact hf
        · exact lt_trans (hchain x hx' i hmem hlt) hf
      · exact hchain x hx' y hy' hxy
    · intro y hy
      rcases Finset.mem_insert.1 hy with rfl | hy'
      · exact le_refl _
      · exact le_of_lt (lt_of_le_of_lt (hle y hy') hij)
  have hcard : (insert j t).card = t.card + 1 := Finset.card_insert_of_notMem hjt
  have hbig : t.card + 1 ≤ incTo f j := by
    rw [← hcard]; exact Finset.le_sup hnew
  have hi' : incTo f i = t.card := hsup
  omega

/-- A decreasing step strictly increases the longest decreasing chain length. -/
lemma decTo_lt_decTo {f : α → β} {i j : α} (hij : i < j) (hf : f j < f i) :
    decTo f i < decTo f j := by
  obtain ⟨t, ht, hsup⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_mem_eq_sup (decChainsTo f i) ⟨{i}, singleton_mem_decChainsTo f i⟩ Finset.card
  simp only [decChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at ht
  obtain ⟨hchain, hmem, hle⟩ := ht
  have hjt : j ∉ t := fun hj => absurd (hle j hj) (not_le.2 hij)
  have hnew : insert j t ∈ decChainsTo f j := by
    simp only [decChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
    refine ⟨?_, Finset.mem_insert_self _ _, ?_⟩
    · intro x hx y hy hxy
      rcases Finset.mem_insert.1 hx with rfl | hx' <;> rcases Finset.mem_insert.1 hy with rfl | hy'
      · exact absurd rfl (ne_of_lt hxy)
      · exact absurd (hle y hy') (not_le.2 (lt_trans hij hxy))
      · have hxi : x ≤ i := hle x hx'
        rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hxi with rfl | hlt
        · exact hf
        · exact lt_trans hf (hchain x hx' i hmem hlt)
      · exact hchain x hx' y hy' hxy
    · intro y hy
      rcases Finset.mem_insert.1 hy with rfl | hy'
      · exact le_refl _
      · exact le_of_lt (lt_of_le_of_lt (hle y hy') hij)
  have hcard : (insert j t).card = t.card + 1 := Finset.card_insert_of_notMem hjt
  have hbig : t.card + 1 ≤ decTo f j := by
    rw [← hcard]; exact Finset.le_sup hnew
  have hi' : decTo f i = t.card := hsup
  omega

/-- **Erdős–Szekeres.**  An injective map on a linearly ordered fintype with more than `r * r`
elements has a strictly monotone subset with more than `r` elements. -/
theorem exists_monotone_chain (f : α → β) (hf : Function.Injective f) {r : ℕ}
    (hcard : r * r < Fintype.card α) :
    ∃ t : Finset α, r < t.card ∧ (IsIncChain f t ∨ IsDecChain f t) := by
  by_contra hcon
  push_neg at hcon
  have hinc : ∀ i : α, incTo f i ≤ r := by
    intro i
    refine Finset.sup_le fun t ht => ?_
    simp only [incChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at ht
    by_contra hgt
    exact (hcon t (by omega)).1 ht.1
  have hdec : ∀ i : α, decTo f i ≤ r := by
    intro i
    refine Finset.sup_le fun t ht => ?_
    simp only [decChainsTo, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at ht
    by_contra hgt
    exact (hcon t (by omega)).2 ht.1
  have hinj : ∀ i ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset α), ∀ j ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset α),
      (incTo f i, decTo f i) = (incTo f j, decTo f j) → i = j := by
    intro i _ j _ hpair
    by_contra hne
    rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hne with h | h
    · rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne (fun hfe => hne (hf hfe)) with hfv | hfv
      · exact absurd (congrArg Prod.fst hpair) (ne_of_lt (incTo_lt_incTo h hfv))
      · exact absurd (congrArg Prod.snd hpair) (ne_of_lt (decTo_lt_decTo h hfv))
    · rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne (fun hfe => hne (hf hfe)) with hfv | hfv
      · exact absurd (congrArg Prod.snd hpair).symm (ne_of_lt (decTo_lt_decTo h hfv))
      · exact absurd (congrArg Prod.fst hpair).symm (ne_of_lt (incTo_lt_incTo h hfv))
  have hmaps : ∀ i ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset α),
      (incTo f i, decTo f i) ∈ (Finset.Icc 1 r ×ˢ Finset.Icc 1 r : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) := by
    intro i _
    simp only [Finset.mem_product, Finset.mem_Icc]
    exact ⟨⟨one_le_incTo f i, hinc i⟩, ⟨one_le_decTo f i, hdec i⟩⟩
  have hle := Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn (fun i => (incTo f i, decTo f i))
    (fun i hi => Finset.mem_coe.2 (hmaps i hi)) (fun i hi j hj h => hinj i hi j hj h)
  have hprod : (Finset.Icc 1 r ×ˢ Finset.Icc 1 r : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)).card = r * r := by
    simp [Finset.card_product, Nat.card_Icc]
  rw [Finset.card_univ, hprod] at hle
  omega

/-- The special case used below: more than nine elements force a monotone quadruple. -/
theorem exists_monotone_four (f : α → β) (hf : Function.Injective f)
    (hcard : 9 < Fintype.card α) :
    ∃ t : Finset α, 4 ≤ t.card ∧ (IsIncChain f t ∨ IsDecChain f t) := by
  obtain ⟨t, ht, hchain⟩ := exists_monotone_chain f hf (r := 3) (by omega)
  exact ⟨t, by omega, hchain⟩

end ErdosSzekeres
